name: hare

text: The hare is a symbolic animal with deep hold on Celtic folklore. In Ireland people believed a hare was a witch in disguise. The animal carried a mythic link to the Cailleach, a witch-like being. When a hare was hurt, a witch in the neighborhood would show the same injury. The same belief runs on the Isle of Man. There a wounded hare always escaped unless shot with a silver bullet, afterwards the witch was found alive or dead with that same wound. In Scotland witches took the form of hares to steal milk, a common target of magical theft. A witch might sneak into a barn and drink from a cow's udder, then turn back to human form if caught. Hares in odd places were read as hidden witches, and a group of hares meant a witches' coven. The creatures strong temper passed to the fairy rabbit, a bold being said to drown people at sea. A traveler who carried earth from home, or from the legendary Tory Island, could survive even this spirit. Ancient records hint at an older meaning. Caesar noted that eating hare flesh was taboo to continental Celts. Dio Cassius told how the warrior queen Boudicca read the future by divination with a hare before battle.
objective: Document the hare as a Celtic witch-symbol with ancient religious roots.
key_results: Record the witch-in-disguise belief in Ireland and the paired-injury lore.
Describe the silver bullet on the Isle of Man and the milk-thief in Scotland.
Note the Caesar taboo and Boudicca's hare divination.
